catalog_quote: 3.4. Supra-segmental items. Stress (loudness), length and pitch are non-contrastive on the phonological word level, being governed by the following principles: 1) Pitch is determined by phrase level features (intonation pattern). Words in isolation are usually pronounced with normal prepause sequence (rising) or statement (falling) intonation. 2) Length is determined mainly by vowel quality, but is also strongly influenced by phonological phrase placement. ... The vowels of syllables taking a phrase stress are usually slightly longer than normal and fortis. 3) Phonological words are normally pronounced with light stress on the first and alternate following syllables. Medial syllables containing consonant or vowel clusters, or medial closed syllables, also tend to be slightly stressed. A compound word generally takes the normal stresses of each of its component parts - i.e. a single grammatical compound word remains two (or more) phonological words. Words within phrases retain their normal stress and length features unless modified by specific phrase level features. [pp.117-118] ... The different analysis of the preceding section is supported by syllabicity and the placement of non-phonemic stress on the peak of the first syllable. [p.102]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-phonemic; a phonological word carries light stress on its first syllable, with alternating (rhythmic) stress on every other following syllable; medial heavy syllables (closed, or containing consonant/vowel clusters) also attract slight stress; each member of a compound keeps its own stress. Elsewhere (p.102) the authors speak of 'the placement of non-phonemic stress on the peak of the first syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternate syllables after the first receive light stress (rhythmic alternation from the initial syllable); medial closed syllables and syllables with clusters also tend to be slightly stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Medial closed syllables / cluster syllables tend to be slightly stressed regardless of the alternating count; compounds behave as two phonological words; phrase-level features (phrase stress, lengthening of phrase-stressed vowels, phrase-final intonation contours on final or penultimate stressed syllable, pp.117-119) can modify word stress and length.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is explicitly about the phonological word; stress described as 'light' and non-contrastive; words in isolation are said to carry normal sequence (rising) or statement (falling) intonation; phrase stress treated separately. Data from the Yangoru (eastern, 'Dialect 1') dialect, Kwahwie village, one main consultant, 1968-1973.
new_statements.identity_note: Freudenburg & Freudenburg 1974 describe the Yangoru ('eastern', their Dialect 1, c. 7,000-7,500 speakers) dialect of Boiken as spoken in Kwahwie village, 3 miles south of Yangoru; Glottolog treats Boikin (boik1241) as one language with several dialects — sub-dialect glottocode for Yangoru not verified here. Laycock 1965's Boikin notes are mainly on the Kwusaun dialect.

sources.note: Sec. 3.4 'Supra-segmental items' (pp.117-118): stress, length and pitch are non-contrastive at the phonological-word level; 'Phonological words are normally pronounced with light stress on the first and alternate following syllables'; medial syllables with clusters or medial closed syllables also tend to be slightly stressed; compounds keep the stresses of each part; p.102 also refers to 'the placement of non-phonemic stress on the peak of the first syllable'. Phrase stress and phrase-final intonation contours described separately (pp.118-119).
